access.edition_or_version: English in Three Satires from Ancient Kashmir, trans. A. N. D. Haksar (Penguin Books India, 2011); text based on the Osmania University Sanskrit edition (1961)

mechanics.premise: A sustained catalogue of clerical greed in 11th-century Kashmir: the appetites of the bureaucratic class are inflated through grotesque exaggeration until the office's stated dignity collapses under the weight of what its holders actually want.
mechanics.point_of_view: Comic-inflating narrator who reports each escalation with straight-faced precision; the derision is carried by accumulation rather than by comment.
mechanics.style_and_devices: Grotesque exaggeration; escalation and accumulation; parody of official self-importance; judgement arranged to be inferred rather than stated.
mechanics.emotional_progression: Amusement at excess -> recognition of systemic greed -> laughter that curdles into exposure.
mechanics.conventions: Classical Sanskrit satire in kavya form; part of Kshemendra's satirical corpus alongside Desopadesa and Kalavilasa; systematic institutional satire in India predating comparable Western canon examples by centuries.
mechanics.critical_reception: Kshemendra is recognized as a major Sanskrit satirist (11th-century Kashmir); the work is a standing reference point for pre-modern Indian institutional satire.
mechanics.verification_note: Existence, author, date (11th-century Kashmir), and satirical character confirmed via Wikipedia API extract (Kshemendra) on 2026-09-24 and the repository's satirical-literature genre file, which analyzes the work's method and its translation limits; Haksar edition identity via publisher catalog metadata. Premise and technique described from these accounts; no passage reproduced. Translation limit: Sanskrit kavya wordplay and courtly bureaucratic diction are only partly carried into English.
